courses.title: Answering awkward questions from little kids
courses.summary: Calm, honest, age-right scripts for the questions that make parents freeze: where babies come from, bodies and touching, death, swear words, and why people look different.
outcomes: Parents use a 4-step method: pause, ask what they think, answer short and true, check in
Parents explain where babies come from at a 3–6-year-old level
Parents respond calmly to body curiosity and teach privacy
Parents talk about death honestly and gently
Parents handle rude words and questions about differences without shaming
courses.guardianNote: For parents and carers. Covers where babies come from (non-graphic, age-appropriate scripts based on UNESCO 2018 guidance), children's body curiosity, death and grief, swear words and slurs, and questions about difference. No explicit content.

lessons.title: The method, and 'Where do babies come from?'

scenes.text: In a Chennai supermarket queue, Kavya (4) points at a pregnant woman: 'Amma, how did the baby get in her tummy?'
Her mother, Deepa, wants to disappear. Instead she breathes, smiles and says, 'Great question! What do you think?'
Kavya says, 'Did she eat it?' Deepa laughs: 'No! Babies grow in a special place inside some mothers' bodies called the uterus. Not the tummy where food goes.'
'Oh,' says Kavya, and asks for a biscuit. Deepa realises: a short true answer was enough.

steps.title: The 4-step method
steps.body:
1. **Pause and stay calm.** Your face teaches more than your words. 'That's a great question.'
2. **Ask what they think** ('What do you think?' / 'Where did you hear that?'). You learn what they *really* want to know.
3. **Answer short and true**, at their level, using correct words. You can add more later.
4. **Check in:** 'Does that answer your question? You can always ask me anything.'

It's fine to say: 'Let me think about that and tell you after dinner' – then do.

steps.title: Age-right answers about babies
steps.body:
**Age 2–4:** 'Babies grow in a special place called the **uterus**, inside the mother's body, below her tummy.'

**Age 4–6, if they ask how it starts:** 'To make a baby, a tiny **egg** from a woman's body and a tiny **sperm** from a man's body join together. Then the baby slowly grows in the uterus for about nine months.'

**How it comes out:** 'Usually through an opening called the **vagina**, which stretches. Sometimes doctors help the baby out with an operation called a **caesarean**.'

Families are also made through adoption, and some babies start with doctors' help (like IVF) – you can mention this if it fits your family.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Myths** ('stork', 'from the hospital', 'God put it there') – children later feel misled and stop asking you.
- **Over-answering** with far more detail than asked.
- **Shaming** ('Chee! Don't ask that!') – this teaches that bodies are dirty and you're not safe to ask, which leaves children vulnerable to wrong information and to abuse.

Children with correct, calm information are **better protected**, not 'spoiled'. This is the approach of UNESCO's 2018 guidance.

steps.title: Keep the door open
steps.body: You will have this talk many times as they grow, a little deeper each time. The goal is not one perfect talk; it's being **the person they come to**.

steps.title: Practise with FAQs
steps.body: Open each question and read a sample answer aloud.

activity.prompt: Questions little children ask – with sample answers

items.a: 'You grew in a special place inside me called the uterus. It's near my tummy but it's not where food goes.' (If adopted: 'You grew inside your birth mother's uterus, and then you came to our family.')

'Most babies come out through an opening between the mother's legs called the vagina – it stretches. Some babies come out through a cut the doctor makes in the mother's belly; it's called a caesarean.'
'Babies grow in a uterus. Most girls are born with a uterus and most boys are not. Both men and women are needed to start a baby – a sperm and an egg.'

items.q: 'How does the sperm get to the egg?' (age 5–6)
items.a: A simple, non-graphic answer: 'When grown-ups decide to have a baby, the sperm comes from the man's penis into the woman's vagina, and swims to the egg. This is something for grown-up bodies only.' Many parents give this answer only if the child keeps asking; it is fine to say 'That's a good question, and I'll tell you more when you're a bit older.'
'She has a baby growing inside her uterus. It will be born in a few months.' Also teach: it's polite not to point or comment on people's bodies loudly.

options: Ask what the child thinks or where they heard it
quiz.why: The answer is "Ask what the child thinks or where they heard it". Reason: You learn what they really want to know. The other choices, such as "Change the subject" and "Give a full biology lecture", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: For a 3-year-old, a good answer to 'Where was I before I was born?' is…
options: 'You grew in a special place inside me called the uterus.'
quiz.why: The answer is "'You grew in a special place inside me called the uterus.'". Reason: Short and true. The other choices, such as "'Don't ask that.'" and "'The stork brought you.'", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Shaming children for body questions tends to…
options: Stop them asking you and leave them less protected
quiz.why: The answer is "Stop them asking you and leave them less protected". Reason: Openness supports safety. The other choices, such as "Keep them safer" and "Make them smarter", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: If you don't know how to answer right away, you can…
options: Say you'll answer after dinner – and do it
quiz.why: The answer is "Say you'll answer after dinner – and do it". Reason: Buying time is fine; follow through. The other choices, such as "Lie" and "Punish the question", do not fit the question.

sources: UNESCO International Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education (2018)

scenes.text: In Pune, Arjun (4) asks during his bath, 'Why does Didi not have a penis?'
His father answers simply: 'Boys usually have a penis and girls usually have a vulva. Different bodies, both normal.'
A week later, Arjun's grandmother sees him touching his penis while watching TV and gasps.
His father calmly tells Arjun, 'Touching your private parts is something we do only in private, like in your room or the bathroom.' Arjun goes back to his blocks.

steps.title: Curiosity is normal
steps.body: Young children are naturally curious about their own and others' bodies: they ask about differences, want to see, play 'doctor', and many touch their own genitals because it feels soothing. **This is a normal part of development** in young children.

steps.title: What to say
steps.body:
- **Differences:** 'Boys usually have a penis and testicles; girls usually have a vulva and vagina. Everyone's body is a little different.'
- **Self-touch:** calmly teach **privacy** ('That's for private places, like your bedroom') and redirect – no shaming, no punishment.
- **Nudity at home:** each family decides; as children grow, teach knocking, closing doors and privacy for themselves and others.

steps.title: Playing 'doctor' with other children
steps.body: Mutual curiosity between children of a **similar age and size** who play willingly happens and is usually not a concern. Calmly stop it, redirect, and use it to teach the **body rules**: private parts are private, we don't touch other people's private parts or ask them to touch ours, and anyone can say no.

steps.title: When to seek advice
steps.body: Talk to your paediatrician or a child psychologist if sexual behaviour is **frequent and hard to redirect**, involves **coercion, force or a big age gap**, causes **distress**, imitates adult sexual acts, or if a child shows knowledge beyond their age. These can be signs that a child has been exposed to sexual content or abuse. In India, **Childline 1098** and **112** can help.

steps.title: Usually typical, or seek advice?
steps.body: Sort these behaviours in 3–6-year-olds.

items.text: Asking why girls and boys look different
Touching own genitals when sleepy or watching TV
Wanting to see a parent in the bathroom
Imitating adult sexual acts in detail
Behaviour that continues despite many calm redirections and causes distress

quiz.q: A 4-year-old touching his penis while watching TV is…
quiz.why: The answer is "Common – teach privacy calmly". Reason: Self-soothing touch is common at this age. The other choices, such as "A reason to punish" and "Proof of abuse", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: The best response to body-difference questions is…
quiz.why: The answer is "Short, calm, correct names". Reason: Correct names, calm tone. The other choices, such as "Laughing at them" and "'We don't talk about that'", do not fit the question.

options: Sexual behaviour involving force or a big age gap
quiz.why: The answer is "Sexual behaviour involving force or a big age gap". Reason: Coercion and age gaps are warning signs. The other choices, such as "Curiosity about the bath" and "Asking why Didi is different", do not fit the question.

options: Some things are done in private places
quiz.why: The answer is "Some things are done in private places". Reason: Privacy, not shame. The other choices, such as "Never talk about bodies" and "Bodies are dirty", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: 'Where did Dadaji go?' – talking about death

scenes.text: In Varanasi, Pihu (5)'s grandfather dies. Everyone is crying. Someone tells her, 'Dadaji has gone to sleep forever.'
That night Pihu refuses to sleep. 'What if I don't wake up too?'
Her mother sits with her: 'Dadaji died. His body stopped working, and it can't start again. He doesn't feel pain or cold. Sleeping is different – when we sleep, we wake up.'
Together they put marigolds by Dadaji's chair and talk about his funny stories.

steps.title: How young children understand death
steps.body: Under about 5–7, many children don't yet understand that death is **permanent**, **happens to all living things**, and means the **body stops working completely**. They may ask the same questions many times, or seem fine and then play 'funeral'. This is how they process it.

steps.title: Use clear words
steps.body:
Say **'died'** and **'dead'**, not 'sleeping', 'lost', or 'gone away' – these can cause fear of sleep or of being left. For example:

*'Dadaji died. His body stopped working – his heart stopped beating and he stopped breathing. He can't feel pain anymore. He won't come back, and we will miss him.'*

Then share your family's beliefs (heaven, rebirth, the soul, or none) as **your family's beliefs** – children can hold both the biological fact and your faith.

steps.title: Questions they ask
steps.body:
- **'Will you die?'** – 'Most people die when they are very, very old. I plan to be here for a long, long time to look after you.'
- **'Did I make it happen?'** – 'No. Nothing you thought, said or did made Dadaji die.'
- **'Can I come to the funeral?'** – Many children benefit from being included, with preparation and a trusted adult beside them.

steps.title: When to get help
steps.body: Grief in children can show as clinginess, tantrums, bedwetting, sleep problems or tummy aches. If these are severe or last many weeks, or your child talks about wanting to die to be with the person, speak to your paediatrician or a child counsellor. Tele-MANAS (**14416**) offers free mental-health support in India, including for grieving parents.

steps.title: Practise
steps.body: Choose what to say.

a.text: Your 4-year-old's pet fish has died. She asks, 'Why isn't Goldie swimming?' What do you say?

choices.label: 'Goldie died. Her body stopped working, so she can't swim or eat anymore.'
choices.feedback: Clear and gentle.

choices.label: 'Goldie is sleeping.'
choices.feedback: This can make her afraid of sleep, or wait for Goldie to wake.

choices.label: Flush it and buy an identical fish secretly
choices.feedback: Children often notice, and it misses a chance to learn about loss.

c.text: Your child seems confused and keeps asking when Goldie will wake up. What now?

choices.label: Gently explain: 'Goldie died. Dead means her body stopped working and won't start again.'
choices.feedback: It's never too late to be clear.

b.text: She asks, 'Will you die too?' What do you say?

choices.label: 'Most people die when they are very, very old. I plan to be here to look after you for a long, long time.'
choices.feedback: Honest and reassuring.

choices.label: 'Never! I'll never die.'
choices.feedback: Well-meant, but not true – later it can shake trust. Reassure without promising the impossible.

d.text: She wants to do something for Goldie. What could you do?

choices.label: Bury Goldie in a pot and plant a flower; share memories
choices.feedback: Simple rituals help children grieve.

choices.label: Tell her to stop being sad
choices.feedback: Sadness is healthy. Let her feel and talk about it.

end.text: Clear words, honest reassurance, small rituals and permission to feel sad help children cope with loss.

quiz.q: Why avoid saying 'He's gone to sleep'?
options: Children may become afraid of sleeping
quiz.why: The answer is "Children may become afraid of sleeping". Reason: Use 'died'. The other choices, such as "It's always fine" and "It's too clear", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Young children may ask the same death question many times because…
quiz.why: The answer is "They're still understanding permanence". Reason: Repetition is processing. The other choices, such as "They're being naughty" and "They didn't hear", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: If a child asks 'Did I make it happen?', you say…
options: 'No, nothing you thought, said or did caused it.'
quiz.why: The answer is "'No, nothing you thought, said or did caused it.'". Reason: Children often feel magical guilt. The other choices, such as "'Maybe'" and "Nothing", do not fit the question.
The answer is "14416". Reason: Free, 24×7 mental-health support. The other choices, such as "100" and "1098", do not fit the question. (Question: India's Tele-MANAS mental-health helpline is…)

story.title: The word from the school bus

scenes.text: In Delhi, Rohan (6) comes home from the school bus and says a swear word he heard from older boys.
His mother, Seema, feels the urge to shout. Instead she asks calmly, 'Where did you hear that word? Do you know what it means?'
Rohan shrugs. 'The big boys laughed when they said it.'
Seema explains: 'It's a rude word that people use to hurt or insult someone. We don't use it in our family. If you hear a word and wonder, ask me – you won't be in trouble.'

steps.title: Why children repeat bad words
steps.body: Young children copy words for the **reaction** they get, to sound grown-up, or because they don't know the meaning. A big shocked reaction makes the word more powerful and more fun to repeat.

steps.title: A calm script
steps.body:
1. **Stay calm** (neutral face).
2. **Ask:** 'Where did you hear it? What do you think it means?'
3. **Explain simply, without repeating or defining graphic meanings:** 'That's a rude word. It's used to hurt people or to talk about bodies in a disrespectful way.'
4. **State the family rule:** 'We don't use that word.' Offer alternatives for big feelings: 'Oh no!', 'I'm so angry!', a silly made-up word.
5. **Thank them for asking** – you want to be their source of answers.

steps.title: Words that hurt groups of people
steps.body: If a child repeats a slur about caste, religion, skin colour, disability, gender or sexuality, explain that it's a word used to **put people down for who they are**, that it causes real hurt, and that in your family everyone is treated with respect.

steps.title: When it's more than a word
steps.body: If a young child uses sexual words together with detailed knowledge of sexual acts, ask gently where they learned it. It may come from exposure to adult content or from abuse; seek advice (paediatrician, child psychologist, **Childline 1098**). Check device and internet settings at home.

steps.title: Model it
steps.body: Children copy what they hear at home. If you swear at traffic, they will too. A quick 'Oops, that was a rude word, I'm sorry' teaches repair.

steps.title: True or false?
steps.body: Check your instincts.

statements.s: A huge shocked reaction makes a bad word less interesting.
statements.why: Big reactions often make children repeat words more.

statements.s: Asking 'Where did you hear that?' helps you understand the situation.
statements.why: It tells you the source and what they know.

statements.s: You must give a detailed definition of every swear word.
statements.why: A simple, non-graphic explanation is enough.

statements.s: Offering alternative words for big feelings helps.
statements.why: Children need ways to express anger.

statements.s: Detailed sexual knowledge in a 5-year-old can be a reason to seek advice.
statements.why: It may indicate exposure or abuse.

quiz.q: First step when your child says a swear word?
quiz.why: The answer is "Stay calm". Reason: Calm reduces the word's power. The other choices, such as "Wash their mouth with soap" and "Scream", do not fit the question.

options: 'It's a rude word used to hurt people; we don't use it in our family.'
quiz.why: The answer is "'It's a rude word used to hurt people; we don't use it in our family.'". Reason: Simple and values-based. The other choices, such as "'I'll tell you when you're 18.'" and "A graphic definition", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: If the word is a slur about a group, you explain…
options: It puts people down for who they are and hurts them
quiz.why: The answer is "It puts people down for who they are and hurts them". Reason: Teach respect for all. The other choices, such as "It's fine at home" and "It's just a joke", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why thank the child for asking?
options: So they keep coming to you with questions
quiz.why: The answer is "So they keep coming to you with questions". Reason: Be their trusted source. The other choices, such as "It's unnecessary" and "To trick them", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: At a metro station in Bengaluru, Zara (4) loudly asks, 'Why is that man in a chair with wheels?'
Her father, Imran, feels embarrassed – but the man smiles.
Imran says, 'Some people's legs don't work in the way ours do, so a wheelchair helps them move. He's going to work, just like us.'
The man says, 'That's right! And it's very fast.' Zara waves. 'Bye!'

steps.title: Curiosity, not rudeness
steps.body: Young children notice differences – skin colour, wheelchairs, hearing aids, hijabs and turbans, size, two dads or a single mum – and ask out loud. They're not being rude; they're learning. **Hushing them** teaches that difference is shameful.

steps.title: What to say
steps.body:
- **Disability:** 'His legs work differently, so a wheelchair helps him get around.' 'She uses her hands to talk – it's called sign language.'
- **Skin colour:** 'People have different skin colours – it comes from something called melanin and from their families. Everyone's skin is good skin.'
- **Families:** 'Some families have a mum and dad, some one parent, some grandparents, some are adopted. What makes a family is that they love and care for each other.'
- **Clothes and faith:** 'He wears a turban because of his religion, Sikhism. Your Nani wears a bindi.'

steps.title: Teach respectful habits
steps.body:
- Talk **about** differences at home, through books and friends.
- Teach: we don't point, stare or touch someone's wheelchair or hair without asking.
- It's okay to say hello! People with differences are people first.
- Avoid words like 'normal' vs 'not normal' – say 'different from us'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Shh! Don't look!' (teaches fear).
- 'We don't see colour' (children do; they need words for it).
- Laughing along with jokes about appearance, caste or religion.

steps.title: Match
steps.body: Match the question to a good answer.

options: People who love and care for each other
Only a mum, dad and two children

early-play.title: Play School (3–4)
early-play.description: Play school learning: phonics A–Z, early science (why is the sky blue?), seasons, feelings and kindness, and good everyday habits.

courses.title: Phonics A to Z: letter sounds
courses.summary: Hear, say and spot the sound each letter makes – a for apple, b for ball – with pictures, songs and games, from A to Z.
outcomes: Child says the main sound for each letter A–Z
Child hears the first sound in familiar words
Child knows vowels a, e, i, o, u
Child matches letters to pictures that start with that sound
courses.guardianNote: For 3–4-year-olds with an adult nearby. Everything can be heard aloud; the child taps, sorts and answers. Short sessions (10 minutes), then practise in real life.

scenes.text: In Thiruvananthapuram, Ammu (4) walks through the market with her mother.
'Apple starts with /a/ – a, a, apple!' Ammu says it too.
A drummer plays at a temple: 'Drum – /d/, /d/, drum!'
At home: 'Egg – /e/, /e/, egg!' Ammu now hunts for sounds everywhere.

steps.title: Letter names and letter sounds
steps.body: Each letter has a **name** (A is 'ay') and a **sound** (A often says **/a/** as in *apple*). For reading, the **sound** matters most. We write sounds between slashes like /a/.
steps.say: Each letter has a name (A is 'ay') and a sound (A often says /a/ as in apple). For reading, the sound matters most. We write sounds between slashes like /a/.

steps.title: A to E
steps.body:
- **A a** says /a/ – apple, ant.
- **B b** says /b/ – ball, bat, bus.
- **C c** says /k/ – cat, cup, cake.
- **D d** says /d/ – dog, drum, duck.
- **E e** says /e/ – egg, elephant.
steps.say: A a says /a/ – apple, ant. B b says /b/ – ball, bat, bus. C c says /k/ – cat, cup, cake. D d says /d/ – dog, drum, duck. E e says /e/ – egg, elephant.

steps.title: Say sounds short
steps.body: Say /b/ quickly, not 'buh'. Clip the sound so it blends easily later: /b/-/a/-/t/ → bat.
steps.say: Say /b/ quickly, not 'buh'. Clip the sound so it blends easily later: /b/-/a/-/t/ → bat.

steps.title: U to Z
steps.body:
- **U u** says /u/ – umbrella, up, under.
- **V v** says /v/ – van, violin, vest.
- **W w** says /w/ – watch, window, web.
- **X x** says /ks/ – usually at the end: bo**x**, fo**x**, si**x**.
- **Y y** says /y/ – yak, yo-yo, yellow.
- **Z z** says /z/ – zebra, zip, zoo (a buzzing bee sound).
steps.say: U u says /u/ – umbrella, up, under. V v says /v/ – van, violin, vest. W w says /w/ – watch, window, web. X x says /ks/ – usually at the end: box, fox, six. Y y says /y/ – yak, yo-yo, yellow. Z z says /z/ – zebra, zip, zoo (a buzzing bee sound).

courses.guardianNote: For 3–4-year-olds with an adult nearby. Everything can be heard aloud; the child taps, sorts and answers. Short sessions (10 minutes), then practise in real life.

scenes.text: On the terrace in Pune, Kiaan (4) looks up. 'Mumma, why is the sky blue?'
Mumma shows him a glass of water in the sunshine making a tiny rainbow on the wall. 'Sunlight has ALL the colours inside it.'
'When sunlight comes through the air, the tiny bits of air bounce the blue light all around the sky – more than the other colours.'
At sunset the sky turns orange. 'Now the light travels through lots more air, and mostly reds and oranges reach us!'

steps.title: Sunlight is a mix
steps.body: Sunlight looks white, but it is a **mix of all the rainbow colours**: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. A rainbow, a prism or a glass of water can split them apart.
steps.say: Sunlight looks white, but it is a mix of all the rainbow colours: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. A rainbow, a prism or a glass of water can split them apart.

steps.title: Air scatters blue
steps.body: Air is made of tiny, tiny bits we cannot see. When sunlight hits them, **blue light gets bounced (scattered) all over the sky much more than red light**. So when we look up, blue comes at us from everywhere – the sky looks blue!
steps.say: Air is made of tiny, tiny bits we cannot see. When sunlight hits them, blue light gets bounced (scattered) all over the sky much more than red light. So when we look up, blue comes at us from everywhere – the sky looks blue!

steps.title: Why sunsets are orange
steps.body: At sunrise and sunset, sunlight goes through much **more air** to reach us. Most of the blue gets scattered away on the way, so the light that reaches our eyes looks **orange and red**.
steps.say: At sunrise and sunset, sunlight goes through much more air to reach us. Most of the blue gets scattered away on the way, so the light that reaches our eyes looks orange and red.

steps.title: Never look at the Sun
steps.body: Never look straight at the Sun – not even with sunglasses. It can hurt your eyes.
steps.say: Never look straight at the Sun – not even with sunglasses. It can hurt your eyes.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: On a sunny day, put a glass of water near a window and look for a rainbow on the wall or floor. Then flip the cards below.
steps.say: On a sunny day, put a glass of water near a window and look for a rainbow on the wall or floor. Then flip the cards below.

Air bounces blue light all over the sky 💙

steps.title: The Earth spins
steps.body: We live on the **Earth**, a giant round ball. The Earth slowly **spins around** like a top. One full spin takes about **one day** (24 hours).
steps.say: We live on the Earth, a giant round ball. The Earth slowly spins around like a top. One full spin takes about one day (24 hours).

steps.title: Day side and night side
steps.body: The **Sun** shines on one side of the Earth – there it is **day**. The other side faces away from the Sun – there it is **night**. As the Earth spins, places move from day into night and back again. The Sun does not really 'go to sleep'!
steps.say: The Sun shines on one side of the Earth – there it is day. The other side faces away from the Sun – there it is night. As the Earth spins, places move from day into night and back again. The Sun does not really 'go to sleep'!

steps.title: The Sun is a star
steps.body: The Sun is a **star** – a giant ball of hot, glowing gas. It looks bigger than other stars because it is so much closer to us. The Moon does not make its own light; it shines because sunlight falls on it.
steps.say: The Sun is a star – a giant ball of hot, glowing gas. It looks bigger than other stars because it is so much closer to us. The Moon does not make its own light; it shines because sunlight falls on it.

steps.title: Try the torch trick
steps.body: In a dark room, shine a torch on a ball. Put a sticker on the ball for your home. Spin the ball slowly – when is your sticker in day, and when in night?

steps.title: Seasons in India
steps.body: Most of India has a hot **summer**, a rainy **monsoon** season, and a cool **winter**, with gentler **spring** and **autumn** in between. (Traditionally India also speaks of six *ritus*.) Different places feel different – hills are cooler, coasts are wetter.

steps.title: Weather words
steps.body: **Sunny, cloudy, rainy, windy, stormy, foggy, hot, cold.** Weather is what the sky and air are like **today**. Ask every morning: 'What's the weather like?'

steps.title: Why does it rain?
steps.body: The Sun warms water in seas, rivers and puddles. Some water turns into invisible **water vapour** and rises up. High in the sky it cools into tiny drops that make **clouds**. When drops join and get heavy, they fall as **rain**.
steps.say: The Sun warms water in seas, rivers and puddles. Some water turns into invisible water vapour and rises up. High in the sky it cools into tiny drops that make clouds. When drops join and get heavy, they fall as rain.

scenes.text: In Lucknow, Zoya (4) helps at her Nana's small shop.

steps.title: Kind words
steps.body:
- **Please** – when we ask for something.
- **Thank you** – when someone gives or helps.
- **Sorry** – when we hurt someone or make a mistake.
- **Excuse me** – to get attention politely.
- **Can I play?** – to join a game.
steps.say: Please – when we ask for something. Thank you – when someone gives or helps. Sorry – when we hurt someone or make a mistake. Excuse me – to get attention politely. Can I play? – to join a game.

steps.title: A real sorry
steps.body: A real sorry has three parts: **say sorry**, **say what you did** ('I spilled juice on your picture'), and **fix it** if you can ('Let me help clean'). Sorry does not mean you are bad – it means you care.
steps.say: A real sorry has three parts: say sorry, say what you did ('I spilled juice on your picture'), and fix it if you can ('Let me help clean'). Sorry does not mean you are bad – it means you care.

steps.title: Why brush?
steps.body: Tiny germs on our teeth love sugar. They make acid that can make **holes** (cavities) in teeth. Brushing removes the germs and food bits.
steps.say: Tiny germs on our teeth love sugar. They make acid that can make holes (cavities) in teeth. Brushing removes the germs and food bits.

steps.title: How to brush
steps.body:
- Brush **twice a day** – morning and before bed.
- Use a **small, soft** toothbrush and a **pea-sized** blob of fluoride toothpaste (for ages 3–6).
- Brush **all sides** of every tooth – front, back and chewing tops – in small circles, for about **2 minutes**.
- **Spit out**, don't swallow the paste. Don't need to rinse a lot.
- A grown-up should help or check brushing until about 7–8 years old.

steps.title: Adding = putting together
steps.body: **4 + 3 = 7** means 4 and 3 more make 7. Start at the bigger number and **count on**: 4… 5, 6, 7.

steps.title: Taking away = some go away
steps.body: **7 − 2 = 5** means you had 7, 2 went away, 5 are left. Start at 7 and **count back**: 6, 5.

steps.title: Use fingers or objects
steps.body:
6 + 2: show 6 fingers, put up 2 more → 8.
9 − 3: show 9 fingers, fold 3 down → 6.

**Number bonds to 10:** 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6, 5+5. Knowing these makes later maths fast.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: When counting on, children often count the starting number again (4 + 3: '4, 5, 6' = 6 ✗). Say the start number in your head, then count the **new** ones: '**4**… 5, 6, 7' ✓.

steps.title: Flat vs solid

steps.title: Five solid shapes

- **Sphere** – ball, laddoo, orange. Rolls in any direction. No flat faces.
- **Cube** – dice, ice cube. 6 square faces, all the same.
- **Cuboid** – brick, matchbox, tiffin box. 6 faces, some long.
- **Cylinder** – tin, pipe, candle. 2 circle faces; rolls and also stacks.
- **Cone** – ice-cream cone, birthday cap. 1 circle face and a point.

steps.title: Helpers in our community
steps.body:
- **Doctor & nurse** – treat us when we are sick or hurt.
- **Police officer** – keeps us safe, helps when we are lost.
- **Firefighter** – puts out fires and rescues people.
- **Farmer** – grows our food.
- **Teacher** – helps us learn.
- **Sanitation worker** – keeps streets clean.
- **Postal worker / delivery person** – brings letters and parcels.
- **Shopkeeper, driver, electrician, plumber, cobbler, tailor, vet, dentist**…

steps.title: Thank them

scenes.text: At a big mall in Gurugram, Mia (5) loses her father.
She remembers: 'Stay where I am. Find a helper.' She goes to a woman at the shop counter.
'My name is Mia Sharma. My papa is Rahul Sharma. His phone is 98…' The shop announces it.
In five minutes Papa is there. 'You did everything right!'

steps.title: Things to know by heart
steps.body:
- Your **full name**.
- Your parent's or carer's **full name**.
- A **phone number** (practise it as a song).
- Your **address** or area and city.

steps.title: If you get lost
steps.body:
1. **Stop** and stay where you are.
2. Look for a **safe helper**: a police officer, a shop worker at the counter, a security guard in uniform, or a mother with children.
3. Tell them your name and your parent's phone number.
4. **Do not go anywhere** with anyone – stay inside the shop or place.

**112** is India's emergency number for police, fire and ambulance. Call it if there is a **fire**, someone is **badly hurt** or **not waking up**, or someone is in **danger**. Say: what happened, where you are, your name. Stay on the phone. **Never call 112 as a joke** – real people need it.

lessons.title: Traffic lights and crossing the road

scenes.text: After school in Bengaluru, Kavin (6) walks home with his Thatha.
At the signal: the red man for walkers is glowing. 'Wait.'
The green man lights up. 'Now look right, look left, look right again.'

steps.title: Traffic light colours
steps.body:
For cars: **Red = stop**, **Yellow/amber = get ready / slow down**, **Green = go**.

For walkers there is often a **red standing person** (wait) and a **green walking person** (cross with care).

steps.title: Stop, look, listen, think
steps.body:
1. **Stop** at the edge of the road (the kerb).
2. **Look right, look left, look right again.** (In India vehicles drive on the left, so the nearest traffic comes from your **right**.)
3. **Listen** for horns and engines.
4. **Think** – cross only when the road is clear.
5. **Walk** straight across – don't run, don't stop in the middle.

steps.title: Road rules for little ones
steps.body:
- **Always hold a grown-up's hand** near roads.
- Use **footpaths**, **zebra crossings**, **subways** or **foot-over bridges**.
- Never cross between **parked cars** – drivers can't see you.
- Never run after a ball onto the road.
- Wear bright clothes at night or on dark rainy days.

lessons.title: Safe in cars, buses and two-wheelers

scenes.text: On a trip from Mumbai to Lonavala, Riaan (5) climbs into his car seat.

steps.title: In a car
steps.body:
- Small children ride in a **child car seat** or booster in the **back seat**, with the belt on, every trip.
- Never sit on someone's lap in a moving car.
- Get in and out on the **footpath side**.
- Don't distract the driver.

steps.title: On a two-wheeler
steps.body: Everyone on a two-wheeler should wear a properly fitting, fastened **helmet**. Hold on tight, keep feet away from the wheels and hot exhaust, and sit still.

steps.title: On the school bus or auto
steps.body:
- Wait for the bus **away from the road** edge.
- Stay **seated**, no standing or pushing.
- Keep **hands and head inside** the window.
- After getting off, never walk right in front of or behind the bus – the driver can't see you. Wait for it to leave or for an adult to help you cross.

courses.guardianNote: Body-safety education for ages 4–6, aligned with UNESCO's 2018 guidance and child-protection practice. Covers correct names for private parts, the 'swimsuit rule', safe vs unsafe touch, surprises vs secrets, No–Go–Tell, choosing trusted adults, online safety basics and 'it is never your fault'. No images or explicit content – only emoji and calm, everyday language. Please do it together and repeat often. Help in India: Childline 1098 · Emergency 112.

scenes.text: Before swimming class in Pune, Coach Neha tells the children about swimsuits.
'Private parts are the parts under your swimsuit – your chest, bottom, and penis or vulva.'
'They are private. Nobody should touch them, look at them or ask you to touch theirs.'
Aisha (5) nods: 'Only to keep me clean or healthy, with Mummy or Papa there!'

steps.title: The swimsuit rule
steps.body: Your **private parts** are the parts covered by your swimsuit or underwear: **chest**, **bottom**, and **penis and testicles** (boys) or **vulva and vagina** (girls). These are their real names – it's okay to say them.

steps.title: My body belongs to me
steps.body:
- My body belongs to **me**.
- Nobody should **touch**, **look at** or **take pictures** of my private parts.
- Nobody should ask me to touch **their** private parts.
- The only exceptions: a parent or carer helping me **wash or use the toilet**, or a **doctor or nurse** checking me **with my parent there**, to keep me healthy.

steps.title: I can say no to any touch
steps.body: Even a hug or kiss from a relative: if you don't want it, you can say 'No thank you' and give a **high five or wave** instead. Grown-ups should respect that.

steps.title: For parents
steps.body: Use a calm, ordinary voice, the same as teaching 'elbow'. Let your child decide about hugs and kisses with relatives – it teaches that *their* no matters. India's child helpline is **1098**; emergency **112**.

buckets: 🚫 Not okay – say NO, go, tell

scenes.text: Aryan (5) in Delhi loves Nani's hugs – they feel warm and safe.
His friend high-fives him after a race – that feels good too.
But one day an older boy pinches him hard and won't stop. Aryan shouts 'Stop!' and runs to his teacher.
His teacher says, 'You did the right thing. That was an unsafe touch.'

steps.title: Safe touches
steps.body: Safe touches make you feel **happy, cared for and safe**: a hug you want, holding hands to cross the road, a pat on the back, a high five, a doctor's check with your parent there.

steps.title: Unsafe touches
steps.body: Unsafe touches **hurt**, or make you feel **scared, confused, uncomfortable or yucky**: hitting, pinching, kicking, touching your private parts, or a touch someone says to keep **secret**.

steps.title: What to do: No, Go, Tell
steps.body:
1. **Say NO** loudly: 'No! Stop!'
2. **Go** – get away to a safe place.
3. **Tell** a trusted grown-up right away.

Even if you couldn't say no or get away, **telling** is always the right thing.

steps.title: Feelings are a warning bell
steps.body: If a touch gives you an 'uh-oh' feeling in your tummy, listen to it. You will **never be in trouble** for telling, even if the person is someone you know, someone in your family, or someone who gave you gifts.

choices.label: Scared I'm in trouble
choices.feedback: You are NOT in trouble. Telling was brave and right.

scenes.text: In Kochi, Diya (5) helps her mother bake a cake for Papa's birthday on Sunday.
'It's a surprise – we'll tell him on Sunday!' Diya feels excited and happy.
Later a neighbour gives her a chocolate and says, 'Don't tell your mother I touched you. It's our secret.'
Diya remembers: surprises are fun and get told soon; this secret feels bad. She tells her mother right away.

steps.title: A surprise
steps.body: A **surprise** is something we keep quiet for a **short time** and then **everyone finds out** – and it makes people **happy**. Birthday gifts, a party, a cake.

steps.title: A secret
steps.body: A **secret** is something someone says you must **never tell**. If a secret makes you feel **worried, scared, sad or confused**, or it's about **touching**, **pictures** or someone **hurting** you – it is an **unsafe secret**. **Always tell** a trusted grown-up.

steps.title: Watch out for tricks
steps.body: Someone might give gifts, sweets or treats, or say 'Your parents will be angry' or 'Nobody will believe you', to make a child keep a secret. These are tricks. Grown-ups who care about you will **never** ask you to keep unsafe secrets.

steps.title: For parents
steps.body: Use the word **surprise** for nice things in your family and avoid asking children to keep 'secrets' from the other parent. Say often: 'You can tell me anything, and I will not be angry with you.'

steps.title: My helping hand
steps.body: A **trusted grown-up** is an adult who keeps you safe, listens to you and helps. Choose **five** – one for each finger – such as a parent, grandparent, aunt or uncle, teacher, school counsellor.

steps.title: How to tell
steps.body: Say: '**I need to tell you something. Someone touched me / showed me something / asked me to keep a secret, and it made me feel bad.**' You don't need perfect words.

steps.title: Keep telling
steps.body: Sometimes a grown-up is busy or doesn't understand. **Keep telling** – tell the next person on your hand – until someone helps you.

steps.title: Numbers for help in India
steps.body:
**1098** – Childline, for children who need help (free, any time).
**112** – Emergency: police, fire, ambulance.

The tuition stopped. Tara felt light again.

steps.title: Never your fault
steps.body: If anyone touches you in an unsafe way, shows you private pictures or asks you to keep an unsafe secret, **it is never, ever your fault** – even if you said yes at first, took a gift, didn't say no, or it happened more than once. The grown-up or older child is responsible.

steps.title: Feelings after
steps.body: You might feel sad, scared, angry, confused or ashamed. These feelings are normal. Telling a trusted grown-up helps the feelings get smaller.

steps.title: Screens too
steps.body: If someone online or on a phone asks you for pictures of your body, shows you pictures of private parts, or says 'keep it secret' – **don't reply, close it, and tell** a trusted grown-up.

steps.title: For parents: if your child tells you
steps.body: **Stay calm**, believe them, thank them for telling, tell them it's not their fault, don't question them repeatedly or confront the person in front of them. Contact **Childline 1098** or **112** for help and guidance; India's POCSO Act protects children and requires such offences to be reported.

lessons.title: Private parts have names too

scenes.text: In Patna, Ravi (3) asks his father, 'What is this called?' while getting dressed.
His father answers calmly, 'That's your penis. It's a private part. Private parts are covered by underwear.'
'Your body belongs to you. Nobody should touch your private parts, except to keep you clean or healthy – like Mummy, Papa or the doctor with us there.'
'If anyone ever does, or makes you feel funny inside, tell me. You will never be in trouble.' Ravi nods and runs to play.

steps.title: Correct names
steps.body:
Child-safety experts recommend teaching **correct names** for all body parts, just like 'elbow' or 'knee':

- Boys have a **penis** and **testicles**.
- Girls have a **vulva** (the outside) and a **vagina** (inside).
- Everyone has a **bottom** (and a **bottom hole**, the anus) and **chest/nipples**.

The **private parts** are the parts covered by underwear (and for girls later a swimsuit top).
steps.say: Child-safety experts recommend teaching correct names for all body parts, just like 'elbow' or 'knee': Boys have a penis and testicles. Girls have a vulva (the outside) and a vagina (inside). Everyone has a bottom (and a bottom hole, the anus) and chest/nipples. The private parts are the parts covered by underwear (and for girls later a swimsuit top).

steps.title: Why correct names?
steps.body: When children know the right words, they can **tell a grown-up clearly** if something hurts or if someone touches them. It also shows that bodies are normal – not something to be ashamed of.
steps.say: When children know the right words, they can tell a grown-up clearly if something hurts or if someone touches them. It also shows that bodies are normal – not something to be ashamed of.

steps.title: My body belongs to me
steps.body:
- My body belongs to me.
- My private parts are private.
- Nobody should touch them or ask to see them, except to keep me clean or healthy (with a trusted grown-up).
- If someone does, I **say no, go away, and tell** a trusted grown-up.
- It is **never my fault**.
steps.say: My body belongs to me. My private parts are private. Nobody should touch them or ask to see them, except to keep me clean or healthy (with a trusted grown-up). If someone does, I say no, go away, and tell a trusted grown-up. It is never my fault.

steps.title: For parents
steps.body: Say the names in a calm, everyday voice. Avoid nicknames that make the part sound shameful. Start a habit of daily 'tell me about your day' chats so telling you things feels normal. If you ever suspect abuse in India, call **1098** (Childline) or **112**.

steps.title: A rainbow plate
steps.body: Different colours of food give different goodness. Try to eat **grains** (rice, roti), **dal or eggs or paneer**, **vegetables**, **fruit**, and **milk or curd**. Drink **water** when thirsty.

steps.title: Safe eating for little ones
steps.body: Cut grapes and cherry tomatoes into small pieces lengthwise, avoid whole nuts and hard sweets for under-5s, and **always sit down to eat** – running while eating can cause choking. Sweets and fizzy drinks are for sometimes, not every day.

lessons.title: Potty learning

scenes.text: Noor (2½) in Srinagar gets a little potty with stars on it.
Her mother reads her a book about a bear who uses the potty.
Noor has many accidents. Mum stays calm: 'Oops, that's okay. Next time, potty!'
After some weeks, Noor says 'Potty!' and goes by herself. 'I did it!'

steps.title: Signs of readiness (often 18 months–3 years)
steps.body:
- Stays dry for 1–2 hours or wakes dry after naps.
- Notices or tells you when nappy is wet or dirty.
- Can pull pants up and down (with help).
- Shows interest in the toilet or copying others.
- Can follow simple instructions.

Every child is different. Starting before the child is ready usually takes longer.
steps.say: Stays dry for 1–2 hours or wakes dry after naps. Notices or tells you when nappy is wet or dirty. Can pull pants up and down (with help). Shows interest in the toilet or copying others. Can follow simple instructions. Every child is different. Starting before the child is ready usually takes longer.

steps.title: Step-by-step plan
steps.body:
1. Get a potty or child seat with a step. Let the child sit on it clothed.
2. Use clear words: **wee (urine)** and **poo**.
3. Sit on the potty at regular times: after waking, after meals, before bath and bed.
4. Watch for signs (wriggling, holding) and say 'Let's go potty!'
5. Teach **wiping front to back** (especially for girls), flushing, and **washing hands with soap**.
6. Praise trying, not just success.
steps.say: 1. Get a potty or child seat with a step. Let the child sit on it clothed. 2. Use clear words: wee (urine) and poo. 3. Sit on the potty at regular times: after waking, after meals, before bath and bed. 4. Watch for signs (wriggling, holding) and say 'Let's go potty!' 5. Teach wiping front to back (especially for girls), flushing, and washing hands with soap. 6. Praise trying, not just success.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Punishing or shaming** accidents – this causes fear and holding, which can lead to constipation.
- Starting during a big change (new baby, moving house).
- Expecting night dryness at the same time – night dryness often comes much later; bedwetting is common even at 5.
steps.say: Punishing or shaming accidents – this causes fear and holding, which can lead to constipation. Starting during a big change (new baby, moving house). Expecting night dryness at the same time – night dryness often comes much later; bedwetting is common even at 5.

steps.title: When to ask a doctor
steps.body: If your child has pain while passing urine or stool, hard stools, blood, or was dry and suddenly starts having many accidents, talk to your paediatrician.
steps.say: If your child has pain while passing urine or stool, hard stools, blood, or was dry and suddenly starts having many accidents, talk to your paediatrician.

lessons.title: My day, sharing and taking turns

scenes.text: At the playground in Goa, Leo (3) and Sana (3) both want the swing.
Leo shouts 'Mine!' and Sana cries.
Leo's mother helps: 'Sana goes first for ten pushes, then Leo. Let's count!'
At ten, Sana jumps off. 'Your turn, Leo!' Both smile.

steps.title: A day has a pattern
steps.body: Wake up → potty and wash → brush teeth → breakfast → play/learn → lunch → nap → play outside → dinner → bath → story → sleep. Picture charts help toddlers know what comes next.
steps.say: Wake up → potty and wash → brush teeth → breakfast → play/learn → lunch → nap → play outside → dinner → bath → story → sleep. Picture charts help toddlers know what comes next.

steps.title: Sharing is hard at 2–3
steps.body: Toddlers are just learning that other people have feelings too. Saying 'Mine!' is normal. Sharing and **turn-taking** need lots of practice and adult help.
steps.say: Toddlers are just learning that other people have feelings too. Saying 'Mine!' is normal. Sharing and turn-taking need lots of practice and adult help.

steps.title: How to teach turns
steps.body:
- Use a timer or count: '10 pushes, then swap.'
- Name feelings: 'You're sad because you want the swing.'
- Praise: 'You gave Sana a turn – that was kind!'
- Let children keep one special toy that doesn't have to be shared.

scenes.text: Newborn Aarav lies in his cradle in Pune. His mother holds a card with bold black stripes about a hand-span from his face.
His eyes lock on to the stripes and stay for a few seconds. 'He sees it!' she whispers.

steps.title: Blurry world
steps.body: A newborn sees best things about **20–30 cm (8–12 inches)** away, roughly the distance from your arm to your face while feeding. Everything else is soft and blurry.

steps.title: Contrast helps
steps.body: Strong **dark-versus-light edges** are easier for new eyes to pick out than pastel shades. That is why stripes, checks, circles and big simple faces hold attention.

steps.title: How to play
steps.body: Hold a card close, wait for baby's eyes to find it, then move it slowly side to side. Stop when baby looks away: that means 'enough'.

steps.title: When to ask
steps.body: If your baby never seems to look at faces or lights, or the eyes seem to wobble or turn constantly after the first weeks, tell your paediatrician.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body: Tummy time is **supervised play on the tummy while baby is awake**. It strengthens neck, shoulders and back, and helps head shape and rolling.

steps.title: Start small
steps.body: Begin from the first days with a minute or two, a few times a day, on your chest or on a firm, flat surface. Slowly build up as baby enjoys it. WHO suggests infants under 1 year get about **30 minutes** of tummy time in total across the day once they are able.

steps.title: Safe sleep is different
steps.body: Tummy time is for play only. For **sleep, always place baby on the back** on a firm, flat surface with nothing loose in the cot.

steps.title: Never alone
steps.body: Never leave baby on the tummy alone or asleep.

steps.title: Touch teaches

steps.title: Check

steps.title: Gentle massage
steps.body: Slow, light strokes with a clean hand while talking can relax baby. Stop if baby cries or turns away. Many families use oil; ask your doctor which is suitable for your baby's skin, especially for newborns or eczema.

steps.title: Bath safety
steps.body: **Never leave a baby alone in water, not even for a moment.** Test water with your elbow (warm, not hot), keep everything you need within reach before you start.

steps.title: Wind-down
steps.body: A bath followed by massage, a feed and a lullaby can become a calm bedtime pattern.

Undress and lower baby gently, holding firmly

Wrap in a towel and dry the folds

steps.title: Why it works

steps.title: Variations
steps.body: Hide a toy under a cloth and let baby find it. Hide behind your hands. Use a soft scarf, never a plastic bag.

steps.title: Separation

steps.title: Choke test
steps.body: If an object fits inside a **toilet-roll tube**, it is too small for a baby under 3. Avoid coins, buttons, batteries and magnets.

steps.title: Safe cupboard
steps.body: Keep **one low cupboard baby-safe** with plastic bowls, lids, wooden spoons, measuring cups. Lock all others.

steps.title: Poisons
steps.body: Phenyl, kerosene, bleach, detergent, medicines and pesticides must be high, locked and in original bottles. If swallowed call a doctor or **112** at once; do not induce vomiting.

steps.title: Games
steps.body: Banging, stacking cups, dropping spoons and finding hidden things. Count the cups aloud.

Everyone empties buckets after use.

steps.title: Water
steps.body: Babies can drown in very small amounts of water, including **buckets**. Empty and turn them over after use. Never leave a baby near a bath, pond or tank.

steps.title: Outdoor play
steps.body: Short trips on a mat in shade, feeling grass or breeze. Protect from midday sun; ask your paediatrician about sunscreen and mosquito protection for young babies.

steps.title: Water play

steps.title: When
steps.body: WHO and Indian guidance: **exclusive breastfeeding for about 6 months**, then add home foods while continuing breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond. Signs: sits with support, good head control, interested in food.

steps.title: General guidance only
steps.body: This is general education, not medical advice. For your own child's health, talk to your paediatrician. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Infant under 1, conscious and not able to cough, cry or breathe
steps.body: Call for help (112). Lay baby face-down along your forearm, head lower than chest, supporting the jaw. Give **5 firm back blows** between the shoulder blades. Turn face up and give **5 chest thrusts** with two fingers on the lower breastbone. Repeat until the object comes out or baby becomes unresponsive.

steps.title: Child over 1
steps.body: Encourage coughing. If not effective, give back blows and then **abdominal thrusts** (Heimlich): stand behind, fist above the belly button, pull inwards and upwards.

steps.title: Unresponsive
steps.body: Call 112 and start CPR if trained.

steps.title: Never
steps.body: Never use blind finger sweeps. Take a hands-on first-aid course.

steps.title: General guidance only
steps.body: This is general education, not medical advice. For your own child's health, talk to your paediatrician. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: What is a fever?
steps.body: Usually a temperature of **38°C (100.4°F)** or higher.

steps.title: See a doctor at once
steps.body: Any fever in a baby **under 3 months**; fever with a rash that does not fade when pressed, stiff neck, trouble breathing, a fit, very sleepy or floppy, refusing feeds, signs of dehydration (no wet nappy in 8 hours, dry mouth, sunken soft spot), or fever over 3 days.

steps.title: At home
steps.body: Dress lightly, offer fluids or feeds, use medicine only as your doctor advises (never aspirin), and keep watching.

steps.title: Febrile fits
steps.body: Fever can trigger a short fit in some young children. Place the child on their side, do not put anything in the mouth and call a doctor.

steps.title: Burns

steps.title: Cuts
steps.body: Press with a clean cloth, raise the limb, wash minor cuts with clean water and cover.

steps.title: Call 112
steps.body: Unconscious, trouble breathing, heavy bleeding, seizure, suspected poisoning, a severe allergic reaction, serious burns.

courses.title: My body is mine: safe touch and unsafe touch
courses.summary: Age-appropriate body safety for 3–6-year-olds: correct body-part names, 'my body belongs to me', safe and unsafe touch, no secrets that hurt, and telling a trusted adult. A guardian's guide is included.
outcomes: Child knows 'my body is mine'
Child knows safe and unsafe touch
Child knows to say no and tell a trusted adult
Grown-up knows how to respond if a child discloses
courses.guardianNote: This course teaches children aged 3–6 body safety using correct names, the underwear rule, 'safe and unsafe touch', and 'say no, go, tell'. It is not explicit. It is age-appropriate and follows UNESCO and WHO guidance on protecting children. Please go through it together, listen without judgement, and talk with your paediatrician if you have concerns. Help: 1098 (Childline) and 112.

scenes.text: Sia does not want to hug a visiting uncle. Her mother says, 'You can wave or high-five instead.'
Sia feels strong and respected.

steps.title: My body belongs to me
steps.body: Your body is yours. You can say 'no' or 'stop' to touch you do not like, even from people you know.

steps.title: Correct names
steps.body: Teach correct names for all parts, including private parts (the parts covered by underwear or a swimsuit), calmly like any other part.

steps.title: Choices
steps.body: Offer a wave, a high-five or a smile instead of forced hugs.

statements.s: My body belongs to me.

quiz.why: It is yours.

quiz.q: A child may say no to…
quiz.why: Body autonomy.
The underwear rule.

scenes.text: Green touch: hugs from family you like, a doctor's check with a parent there.
Red touch: anyone touching private parts, or touch that hurts or feels wrong.

steps.title: Safe touch
steps.body: Touch that is caring: help with a bath from a parent, a doctor's check with a parent present, a hug you want.

steps.title: Unsafe touch
steps.body: Touching or looking at private parts without a good caring reason, or touch that hurts or scares. It is **never** the child's fault.

steps.title: No secrets
steps.body: A surprise party is a happy secret that ends soon. A secret that makes you feel scared or sad is **not** kept; tell a trusted adult.

items.text: A hug from Dadi that I like

quiz.why: Responsibility lies with the adult.

scenes.text: A big boy at the park asks Raj to go behind a wall.
Raj says 'No!' runs to his teacher and tells her. She thanks him.

steps.title: Say, go, tell
steps.body: 1) Say **no** loudly. 2) **Go** away to safety. 3) **Tell** a trusted adult. Keep telling until someone listens.

steps.title: Trusted adults
steps.body: Choose five people (parent, grandparent, teacher...). Draw them on a hand, one per finger.

steps.title: Help
steps.body: Childline **1098** and emergency **112** are free. In India, the POCSO Act 2012 protects children.

steps.title: For guardians
steps.body: If a child tells you: stay calm, believe them, thank them, tell them it is not their fault, do not confront alone, and seek help from a paediatrician, 1098 or the police. This is general education, not legal advice.

choices.label: Keep the secret

c.text: Remember: telling is always the right thing. Try again.
